Recruitment should not feel like paying a premium every time someone accepts an offer.

That model works. But it is not the only model.

At hrcg recruitment and HR Corner Group, we are opening a limited number of Recruitment-as-a-Service (RaaS) partnerships for companies that need consistent hiring support without building a larger internal recruitment team or paying traditional agency fees role by role.

Instead of treating every vacancy as a separate transaction, we become part of your recruitment capability.

Monthly retainer from AED 8,000–25,000, depending on hiring volume, complexity and scope.
What sits behind it?
→ End-to-end recruitment ownership
→ Role scoping and success profiling
→ UAE + international market mapping
→ Active headhunting — because posting a vacancy and hoping is not a sourcing strategy
→ Structured interviews and scorecards
→ Offer and negotiation support
→ CliftonStrengths analysis for senior candidates where appropriate
→ Ongoing workforce and capability advisory

And there is another conversation I am very happy to have:
Show me your current recruitment engagement and commercial model.
We will review it and see whether we can create something more commercially effective, more flexible and better aligned with the actual hiring outcome you need.
As I see it, the product is not really recruitment. The product is capability acquisition. A vacancy you might have right now is simply one possible solution. Sometimes you need permanent talent. Sometimes contract. Sometimes fractional expertise. Sometimes a consultant. Sometimes AI or automation changes the requirement completely.

That is why we start with the business need, not the job description.
Very Simon Sinek: Start with WHY the capability needs to exist.

Then decide WHO — and how — should deliver it.

If you are hiring repeatedly across the UAE, GCC or internationally, scan the QR code, request the full brochure, or message me directly for a complimentary consultation.

Let’s see whether your recruitment model can work harder for you.

HRCG Recruitment 
Recruitment. Reconsidered.

𝗔 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺.
But that is exactly what happens in a lot of growing companies.
Sales needs an answer from Product.
 Product needs context from Customer Success.
 Finance needs numbers from Operations.
 Operations needs the founder to clarify priority.
So the founder becomes the integration layer.
Everything works.
Until it doesn’t.
The symptoms usually look like:
→ decisions waiting for one person
 → the same questions being answered repeatedly
 → updates living across Slack, email and meetings
 → teams unsure who actually owns the next step
 → the founder carrying context that should live in the system
At that point, the problem is not simply “we need better project management.”
It is:
How do we remove unnecessary dependence on the founder without losing judgment?
That is where I think good Operations / Chief of Staff work becomes valuable.
The job is to turn founder-held context into:
Clear ownership
 Decision rules
 Escalation thresholds
 Reliable handoffs
 Shared operating data
 Automation where repetition adds no value
And increasingly, AI can help with part of that layer:
Context gathering → exception detection → summaries → recommendations → routing
But the operating logic still matters more than the model.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀.
𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 𝗮𝘀 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲.
That is the kind of work I’ve spent most of my career doing — and the part I’m now increasingly combining with hands-on AI and automation.
If you’re hiring for Chief of Staff, Founder’s Office, Business Operations, Program / Implementation Management or AI Ops — remote, contract or part-time — happy to talk.

Sometimes the HealthTech roadmap isn't the problem.

The team available to deliver it is.
A HealthTech company can have a clear roadmap:
A new patient app.
An EHR integration.
AI capabilities.
Platform modernization.
Better analytics.
A major customer implementation.
And still struggle to deliver on time.
Not because the engineering team isn't capable.
Because they're already at capacity.
Then hiring starts.
Java developers.
.NET engineers.
Data engineers.
Cloud specialists.
QA automation.
AI/ML talent.
And suddenly, a product deadline has also become a recruitment deadline.
This is something I think HealthTech companies need to plan for earlier.
Because finding a developer isn't necessarily difficult.
Finding someone with the right technical depth, healthcare context and availability — at the moment the roadmap needs them — is a very different challenge.
Sometimes permanent hiring is the right answer.
Sometimes you need contract capacity for 6 months.
Sometimes you need a niche specialist for one critical project.
The hiring model can change.
But the objective shouldn't:
Don't let an open position become a product bottleneck.
Over the next few weeks, I'll be sharing more about the technology hiring challenges I see across HealthTech and Healthcare IT — and how companies can build engineering capacity without compromising on talent quality.

A COO put it to me like this: "During covid we did the same revenue with a team of 100. Now we need to do it with 30."

It surfaces an underlying question that confuses some boards: is AI an efficiency play or a growth play?

The latest data says most companies end up on one side. PwC went back to 351 CEOs this summer with their CEO snapshot. 18% saw AI decrease their costs. Only 4% saw it increase revenue, and 9% got both. Meaning, the market is currently leaning towards the cost side.

My clients don't treat it as a choice. The brief I get when I ask them about strategic priorities is usually both: do the same revenue without growing the team, or increase growth without hiring.

Looking at the projects I did, most initiatives have room for both. Take a customer service bot. On its own it is an efficiency play, because it absorbs part of the capacity you would otherwise staff. But that same bot sits in the middle of thousands of customer conversations. When someone asks about a return, it can suggest a better replacement or point to items that fit what they already own. The same investment now has a revenue side.

The catch is that you need to be strict about the value from day one. The revenue side adds development cost, and it only pays back if the mechanism is defined before you build. I have also seen the reverse, where the revenue features came first, and neither play delivered.

The rule I use in business cases: saved time only becomes money when a hire gets cancelled or delayed, when the same team handles more volume, or when external spend goes down. And count the full cost, including the people who supervise the AI. In a conservative scenario, year one is often negative.

What I would tell any leadership team wrestling with this:
- Decide the primary play per use case. Efficiency and growth can live in the same initiative, but one of them carries the business case.
- Give the revenue side its own small budget and a number it has to hit, and expand it only when that number shows up.
- Write the value mechanism down before development starts.

A simple test for your next AI steering meeting: pick one initiative and ask which hire, which volume target, or which vendor contract it touches.

Would You Take a Lower-Paid Consultancy for a Shot at a Roster Spot? Here's How to Think About It

A reader asked us this exact question last week: turn down a fully-loaded staff offer, or take a six-month consultancy at less than half the pay because it might get you "in the door" with an agency you actually want to work for?
It's a real trade-off, and it's worth thinking through with the actual numbers instead of the story we tell ourselves about it.

Start with what a consultancy actually is, on paper. Under the UN's own administrative instruction governing consultants (ST/AI/2013/4), a consultant is "neither a staff member... nor an official", capped at 24 months of service in any 36-month period, with no paid leave of any kind, no UN-arranged health or life insurance, no training at UN expense, and no pension participation. The day rate can look competitive next to a staff salary. The total package underneath it is a different number entirely.

The roster part is where people talk themselves into it, and here's the honest read: that same instruction states a consultant is "not eligible to apply for or be appointed to any position in the Professional and higher categories... within six months of the end of their current or most recent service." That's not a shortcut into a staff role for most of the UN Secretariat; it's a mandatory pause written directly into the policy. (Rules vary by entity: UNFPA's own consultant policy, for one, requires no break before moving into a staff post there. Check the specific agency, not the system as a whole.)

So if the roster isn't the real prize, what is? The same thing that decides most hiring, consultancy or not: whether the person making the decision already knows your work. Referral research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found referred candidates make up just 6% of applicants at a typical employer, but 29% of actual hires, and are 14 points more likely to get an offer once they reach that stage. A consultancy doesn't buy a formal advantage. Six months of a hiring manager watching you work might buy an informal one.

Before taking the pay cut, it's worth answering three questions instead of one: Will this role put you in direct contact with the person who'd be hiring for the job you actually want, or just adjacent to their team? Can you afford the gap in the months, the missing benefits, the tax hit, without it changing the decision you make under pressure later? Does this specific agency's policy let consultancy lead anywhere, or does it require a break that cancels out the head start?

None of that makes the answer yes or no for you. It just means the decision is worth making with the actual mechanics in front of you, not the version of the story where "roster" quietly means "guarantee."

Have you taken a lower-paid contract as a bet on what it might lead to? Did it pay off the way you expected?

INDEPENDENT ARTISTS: AI CAN HELP YOU THINK LIKE A LABEL BEFORE YOU CAN AFFORD A LABEL’S LEGAL TEAM.

If you’re an emerging artist thinking about starting your own record label, hiring a manager, negotiating distribution, or reviewing contracts, legal costs can become a major obstacle.

An entertainment attorney can be extremely valuable, but a $5,000 retainer may not be realistic for an artist who is still building revenue.

That’s where AI can help.

With ChatGPT or Claude projects, artists can create a dedicated music-business research environment and provide authoritative reference material such as Black’s Law Dictionary, relevant sections of the U.S. Code, Copyright Office resources, state business laws, and their own agreements.

You can instruct AI to help:

• Explain contract terminology
• Review management agreements
• Identify royalty, publishing, master ownership, recoupment, exclusivity, option, licensing, and termination clauses
• Break down manager commissions and sunset clauses
• Prepare questions for an attorney
• Research how to structure an independent label
• Flag provisions that deserve professional review

That requires a relatively small investment compared with immediately spending thousands of dollars every time a contract crosses your desk.

This becomes especially important when hiring a manager. Before signing anything, understand exactly what percentage they receive, what income they participate in, how long the agreement lasts, their authority, expenses, exclusivity, and your termination rights.

Artists should also research potential conflicts of interest. Entertainment attorneys, managers, agencies, publishers, distributors, and major labels often operate within the same professional networks. That does not automatically mean anyone is acting improperly, but you should know who represents whom and whose interests are being protected.

AI should not replace a qualified entertainment attorney when serious money or rights are at stake.

But it can help you become a much more informed client.

Understand your contracts. Protect your masters. Know your publishing. Choose your manager carefully. Build your label intelligently.

Use AI to educate yourself before someone asks for your signature.

Disclaimer: Educational information only, not legal advice. AI can make mistakes. Consult a qualified attorney regarding your specific circumstances.

🇮🇳 India's GCC Boom Is a Major Growth Engine
India's Global Capability Centre (GCC) sector is a standout driver within this story. EY projects India's domestic GCC market will reach roughly $110 billion by 2030, up from about $45 billion, with the country hosting around 2,400 GCCs employing 4.5 million people — a sharp jump from roughly 1.9 million employed today. More recent industry tracking shows India's GCC market has already grown from $30 billion in 2019 to around $64 billion in 2024, expanding at close to 10% annually, with GCCs now accounting for over 40% of gross office leasing across India's top seven cities.

Rising demand for specialized and niche skills in IT, healthcare, and engineering that generalist hiring models can't fill fast enough

What This Means for the Industry
Growth won't be uniform. Firms and hiring leaders who specialize — particularly around GCC enablement, niche technical talent, and total talent management — are positioned to capture a disproportionate share of this expansion. Commoditized, generalist staffing models will feel the most pressure.

RPA + AI/ML: The Future of Intelligent Automation! 

Robotic Process Automation (RPA) has revolutionized business operations by automating repetitive, rule-based tasks. But what happens when we combine RPA with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML)? We get Intelligent Automation—a game-changer for businesses looking to automate complex, decision-driven processes!
Here’s how AI/ML enhances RPA and takes automation to the next level: 

AI-Powered Document Processing
Traditional RPA struggles with unstructured data like invoices, contracts, and emails. AI bridges this gap using:

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) – Extracts text from scanned documents

Natural Language Processing (NLP) – Understands context in emails & chat messages

Machine Learning Models – Classifies and processes documents intelligently
Example: Automating invoice processing by extracting details, validating them, and updating ERP systems!
Chatbots & Conversational AI
RPA alone can’t handle dynamic conversations, but when integrated with AI-powered chatbots, businesses can:

Automate customer support with AI chatbots

Process requests like ticket creation, refunds, and FAQs

Provide 24/7 self-service without human intervention

Example: AI-driven bots can understand customer intent, trigger RPA workflows, and resolve issues faster!
Predictive Analytics for Decision-Making
While RPA follows predefined rules, AI/ML enables predictive decision-making by analyzing past data patterns.

 Fraud Detection – AI models identify anomalies in transactions

 Demand Forecasting – ML predicts future inventory needs

 Customer Insights – AI analyzes behavior to personalize experiences
Example: An RPA bot can process claims, while AI flags suspicious ones for manual review, reducing fraud risks!
Intelligent Email & Text Processing
AI-powered RPA can read, understand, and act on emails automatically:

Extract key details from emails, attachments, and PDFs

Categorize messages and trigger appropriate workflows

Auto-respond to customer inquiries with context-aware replies

Example: An AI bot can read incoming resumes, extract skills, and update an HR database automatically!

Hyperautomation: The Ultimate Goal

 Hyperautomation = RPA + AI/ML + Analytics + Advanced Automation

 It enables end-to-end business automation, reducing manual intervention significantly

 Businesses achieve higher efficiency, cost savings, and improved customer experiences
Example: AI-powered RPA bots can automate entire supply chain operations, from order processing to delivery tracking!

The EU AI Act is live. Since 2 August 2026, the transparency rules apply to every company using AI in the EU.

I completed the certified EU AI Act training by WBS.LEGAL. Here is what leadership teams need to know now.

These are my key learnings:

1. AI is regulated now
The Act puts duties on deployers. If an employee is using a private ChatGPT account for work, the company becomes a deployer. Without an inventory of the AI tools and a role for each tool, you cannot tell which duties apply, and you are responsible for every violation.

2. AI literacy is mandatory
Art. 4 requires documented AI literacy for everyone working with AI, and management holds the burden of proof. If you haven't documented your training when a regulator asks, every other violation counts as careless. Training should cover mistakes such as wrong facts in AI copy, poisoned code and leaked customer data.

3. Labeling content needs an owner
Photorealistic AI product images, AI voice overs, chatbots and AI written text all trigger disclosure duties. AI text needs no label when a human checks facts, quotes and sources before publishing. A quick read through does not qualify. A labeling matrix in your AI policy, handed to marketing, prevents costly mistakes.

4. AI content does not create copyright
The only way to protect an AI-generated logo or campaign visual is a trademark. Register the assets that carry your brand, and keep humans in the creative process where you need copyright.

5. Enforcement starts with a complaint, not a fine
The maximum fine of 35M EUR or 7% of turnover is for the big players. For everyone else, the pattern will follow GDPR: a complaint, an inquiry from the Bundesnetzagentur, and document requests. Your preparation decides whether that inquiry takes an afternoon or a quarter. Keep these documents up to date: your AI inventory, internal AI policy, training records, and vendor contracts including data processing agreements.

6. Start on the high-risk rules now
From December 2027, AI in hiring, credit scoring and insurance requires risk management, technical documentation, logging and human oversight. This is not limited to LLMs: classic machine learning counts too. A self-trained classifier that scores applicants or loan requests is an AI system under the Act. Identify those use cases today and keep the final decision with a human. Retrofitting oversight into a running HR process costs more than designing it in. 

Where does AI governance sit in your organization today: board, IT or nowhere yet?
